questions.text: How long have you had difficulty with erections, and did it develop gradually or suddenly?
questions.purpose: Sudden onset suggests psychological or vascular event; gradual onset suggests organic progressive disease

questions.text: Is the problem present in all situations (global) — including during masturbation and on waking — or only with a partner (situational)?
questions.purpose: Situational ED suggests psychogenic cause; global ED across all contexts points to organic vascular or neurological aetiology
options: Only with partner — able to have morning erections and masturbate normally
Only with partner — no morning erections
In all situations, including masturbation and on waking
Partial erections only in all situations

questions.text: Do you have any cardiovascular risk factors — hypertension, diabetes, high cholesterol, obesity, or do you smoke?
questions.purpose: Vascular risk factors are the most common organic cause of ED; ED may also be a sentinel marker for occult cardiovascular disease

questions.text: Have you had any recent chest pain, shortness of breath on exertion, or been told you have heart disease?
questions.purpose: Established cardiac disease requires cardiovascular risk stratification before prescribing PDE5 inhibitors

questions.text: Are you taking any medications that may cause ED — antihypertensives (beta-blockers, thiazides), antidepressants, antipsychotics, or antiandrogens?
questions.purpose: Many medications cause ED as a side effect; identifying them may allow substitution without further investigation

questions.text: Do you have any symptoms suggesting low testosterone — reduced libido, fatigue, reduced body hair, or loss of muscle?
questions.purpose: Hypogonadism is a correctable hormonal cause of ED

questions.text: Are you experiencing significant stress, anxiety, depression, or relationship difficulties?
questions.purpose: Psychological factors are the leading cause of ED in younger men; identifying them guides psychosexual therapy referral
